current_disclosures.section: Legal and Regulatory > THE GOLDMAN SACHS GROUP, INC. AND SUBSIDIARIES
current_disclosures.summary: The firm faces higher and more stringent capital requirements due to Basel III reforms, including the implementation of the Supervisory Capital Buffer (SCB) and G-SIB surcharge, with the G-SIB surcharge expected to increase from 3.0% to 3.5% on January 1, 2026, potentially further increased by a July 2023 FRB proposal.

comparisons.peer_topic: Legal entity structure and restrictions on intercompany fund transfers
comparisons.peer_summary: The parent company depends on dividends and loans from subsidiaries for liquidity but faces legal, regulatory, and contractual restrictions on transferring funds, including dividend limits, capital requirements, and resolution planning arrangements.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Bank of America disclose that regulatory and legal restrictions limit the efficient movement of capital and liquidity among affiliates, thereby increasing consolidated requirements. Goldman Sachs explicitly cites 'ring fencing' and the inability to 'efficiently move capital and liquidity among our affiliated entities' as a result of government steps to protect local creditors (gs_2024_1A_P055_S002, gs_2024_1A_P055_S003). Similarly, Bank of America states there are 'legal, regulatory, contractual and other limitations on our ability to utilize liquidity from one legal entity to satisfy the liquidity requirements of another' (bac_2024_1A_P026_S003) and that bank/broker-dealer subsidiaries face restrictions on using funds to fund their businesses or transact with affiliates (bac_2024_1A_P027_S002).

sentences.text: Concerns about protecting clients and creditors of branches and subsidiaries of financial institutions that are located outside of the country in which such branches or subsidiaries are located or do business have caused or may cause a number of governments and regulators to take additional steps to "ring fence" or require internal total loss-absorbing capacity (which may also be subject to "bail-in" powers, as described below) at those branches and subsidiaries in order to protect clients and creditors of those branches and subsidiaries in the event of financial difficulties involving those branches and subsidiaries.

The result has been and may continue to be additional limitations on our ability to efficiently move capital and liquidity among our affiliated entities, or to Group Inc., including in times of stress, thereby increasing the overall level of capital and liquidity required by us on a consolidated basis.

Legal entity liquidity is an important consideration as there are legal, regulatory, contractual and other limitations on our ability to utilize liquidity from one legal entity to satisfy the liquidity requirements of another, including the parent company, which could result in adverse liquidity events.

Our bank and broker-dealer subsidiaries are subject to restrictions on their ability to lend or transact with affiliates, minimum regulatory capital and liquidity requirements and restrictions on their ability to use funds deposited with them in bank or brokerage accounts to fund their businesses.

comparisons.peer_summary: Citigroup Inc.'s liquidity depends on payments from subsidiaries, which may be restricted by capital adequacy rules, regulatory stress tests, or affiliate transaction limits for broker-dealer and bank subsidiaries.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures address how regulatory restrictions on intercompany transfers impact the parent company's liquidity. Goldman Sachs notes that limitations on moving capital 'among our affiliated entities' increase consolidated capital needs (gs_2024_1A_P055_S003). Citigroup similarly explains that its liquidity depends on payments from subsidiaries, which are restricted by 'capital adequacy or other liquidity, regulatory or contractual restrictions' and 'inter-affiliate arrangements' (c_2024_1A_P113_S003). Both highlight that these restrictions can impede the parent's ability to fund obligations.

sentences.text: The result has been and may continue to be additional limitations on our ability to efficiently move capital and liquidity among our affiliated entities, or to Group Inc., including in times of stress, thereby increasing the overall level of capital and liquidity required by us on a consolidated basis.

Several of Citi's U.S. and non-U.S. subsidiaries are or may be subject to capital adequacy or other liquidity, regulatory or contractual restrictions on their ability to provide such payments, including any local regulatory stress test requirements and inter-affiliate arrangements entered into in connection with Citigroup Inc.'s resolution plan.

Citigroup Inc.'s broker-dealer and bank subsidiaries are subject to restrictions on their ability to lend or transact with affiliates, as well as restrictions on their ability to use funds deposited with them in brokerage or bank accounts to fund their businesses.

comparisons.peer_summary: Payments from JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and the IHC to the Parent Company are limited by regulatory capital, liquidity, and distribution restrictions.
comparisons.comparison: Both firms disclose that regulatory capital and liquidity requirements restrict the flow of funds from subsidiaries to the parent. Goldman Sachs states that 'ring fencing' leads to 'additional limitations on our ability to efficiently move capital and liquidity among our affiliated entities' (gs_2024_1A_P055_S003). JPMorgan Chase specifies that 'JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is subject to regulatory restrictions on its dividend distributions, as well as capital adequacy requirements... and liquidity requirements and other regulatory restrictions on its ability to make payments to the Parent Company' (jpm_2024_1A_P097_S002). Both identify these constraints as increasing the capital/liquidity needed at the consolidated or parent level.

sentences.text: The result has been and may continue to be additional limitations on our ability to efficiently move capital and liquidity among our affiliated entities, or to Group Inc., including in times of stress, thereby increasing the overall level of capital and liquidity required by us on a consolidated basis.

JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is subject to regulatory restrictions on its dividend distributions, as well as capital adequacy requirements, such as the Supplementary Leverage Ratio ("SLR"), and liquidity requirements and other regulatory restrictions on its ability to make payments to the Parent Company.

The IHC is prohibited from paying dividends or extending credit to the Parent Company if certain capital or liquidity thresholds are breached, or if limits are otherwise imposed by the Parent Company's management or Board of Directors.

comparisons.peer_topic: Holding company structure and subsidiary payment restrictions
comparisons.peer_summary: As a holding company, the firm depends on subsidiary payments to fund obligations and dividends, but regulatory, tax, and legal restrictions, including ring-fencing measures, may limit or block these fund transfers.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley explicitly mention 'ring fencing' as a regulatory measure that restricts the flow of funds. Goldman Sachs describes efforts to 'ring fence' branches and subsidiaries as causing limitations on moving capital and liquidity (gs_2024_1A_P055_S002). Morgan Stanley similarly notes that laws and regulations permit regulatory bodies to 'block or reduce, the flow of funds to the Parent Company... including steps to "ring fence" entities by regulators outside the U.S.' (ms_2024_1A_P049_S003). Both disclosures frame this as a risk to the parent company's ability to access necessary funds.

sentences.text: Concerns about protecting clients and creditors of branches and subsidiaries of financial institutions that are located outside of the country in which such branches or subsidiaries are located or do business have caused or may cause a number of governments and regulators to take additional steps to "ring fence" or require internal total loss-absorbing capacity (which may also be subject to "bail-in" powers, as described below) at those branches and subsidiaries in order to protect clients and creditors of those branches and subsidiaries in the event of financial difficulties involving those branches and subsidiaries.

In particular, many of our subsidiaries, including our bank and broker-dealer subsidiaries, are subject to laws, regulations and self-regulatory organization rules that, in certain circumstances, limit, as well as permit regulatory bodies to block or reduce, the flow of funds to the Parent Company, or that prohibit such transfers or dividends altogether, including steps to "ring fence" entities by regulators outside the U.S. to protect clients and creditors of such entities.
These laws, regulations and rules may hinder our ability to access funds that we may need to make payments on our obligations.
